lesson.title: Weighing Electrons: How PES Reveals an Atom's Inner Structure
lesson.summary: Photoelectron spectroscopy fires high-energy photons at atoms to eject electrons and measures their leftover kinetic energy, letting chemists directly measure how tightly each electron is bound and confirm electron configurations.
lesson.body:
The photoelectric effect chapter showed that light striking a metal surface can eject electrons, with kinetic energy determined by KE_max = hf - phi. Photoelectron spectroscopy, often abbreviated PES, takes that exact same idea and turns it into one of chemistry's most direct windows into atomic structure. Instead of shining modest-energy visible or ultraviolet light on a solid metal to knock out its most loosely held electrons, PES uses higher-energy photons, typically ultraviolet or X-ray radiation, aimed at individual gas-phase atoms or molecules. Because these photons carry more energy, they can eject not just the outermost valence electrons but also electrons buried deep in inner shells, close to the nucleus.

The bookkeeping is identical in spirit to the photoelectric effect: energy is conserved, so the photon's energy is split between freeing the electron and giving it speed. Instead of a work function, chemists talk about the binding energy, BE, the energy required to remove one specific electron from the atom entirely. The relationship rearranges to BE = hf - KE, where hf is the known, fixed energy of the photon source, and KE is the kinetic energy of the ejected electron, measured directly by an electron energy analyzer. Since hf is known precisely, measuring KE for each ejected electron lets chemists calculate exactly how tightly that electron was held, its binding energy, without ever seeing the electron configuration directly.

Binding energy is not the same for every electron in an atom, and that is exactly what makes PES useful. Electrons in shells close to the nucleus, especially 1s electrons, experience the full attractive pull of the nucleus with very little shielding from other electrons, so they are held extremely tightly and have large binding energies. Electrons farther out, in the valence shell, are shielded by all the electrons underneath them and are held far more loosely, giving them much smaller binding energies. Every subshell, 1s, 2s, 2p, and so on, has its own distinct binding energy, so a PES spectrum comes out as a series of separate peaks rather than one smooth signal.

Neon, with the electron configuration 1s2 2s2 2p6, is a clean example. Experimentally, its 1s electrons have a binding energy of about 84.0 MJ per mole, its 2s electrons about 4.68 MJ per mole, and its 2p electrons about 2.08 MJ per mole, a value that matches neon's well known first ionization energy of 2080 kJ/mol almost exactly, since removing a 2p electron is exactly what ionization measures. The enormous gap between the 1s peak and the 2s/2p peaks, roughly eighteen-fold, is a direct experimental signature of the difference between a deeply buried core electron and much more loosely held outer electrons, the same core versus valence distinction that shapes so much of periodic table chemistry.

High-resolution photoelectron spectroscopy was pioneered by the Swedish physicist Kai Siegbahn, who won the 1981 Nobel Prize in Physics for developing the technique into a precise tool for chemical analysis. Beyond confirming electron configurations, PES data can be read almost like a bar code for an element, with the number of peaks, their spacing, and their relative heights all carrying information, which is exactly the skill built up in the next chapter on interpreting PES data.
